newEntries.standardEnglish: Ah (ASV, NRSV, NJPS at 1:4, 1:24); Woe (ASV/NRSV in most 'woe-oracle' openings, e.g. 5:8; 29:1; 45:9)
newEntries.wohChoice: 'Woe' for hôy throughout Isaiah: vocative 'Woe, sinful nation' (1:4), as 'Woe, Ariel' (29:1); 'Woe to …' before a participle or preposition (29:15; 45:9, 10; the woe-series of 5:8-22); absolute 'Woe!' introducing a divine threat (1:24).
newEntries.rationale: hôy is the cry of the funeral lament (1 Kgs 13:30; Jer 22:18; 34:5), which the eighth-century prophets turned into the opening of the woe-oracle against the living (Westermann, Basic Forms of Prophetic Speech, 1967; Gerstenberger, 'The Woe-Oracles of the Prophets', JBL 81, 1962; Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, on 5:8). The English versions render it by context, 'Ah' where it stands alone and 'Woe' where it is followed by 'to' or a participle, so the same Hebrew word appears under two English words in one book. The signed-off Isaiah chapters already print 'Woe' at 29:1, 15 and 45:9, 10, and the wave I-1 ruling extends that rendering to every hôy in Isaiah so that readers can trace the form. At 1:24 the cry introduces YHWH's threat against his adversaries; NJPS 'Ah' is the more idiomatic English there, and the uniform 'Woe!' is accepted for consistency and noted in commentary. The claim is direct: 'woe' is a standard lexical equivalent of hôy (BDB, HALOT), and no interpretive reading is added. Recommend adding the signed-off sites ISA-29:1, 29:15, 45:9, 45:10 to appliesTo at merge (their paragraph glossaryRefs were not edited in this wave).

newEntries.lemma: ʾāḏôn 'lord, master', singular with the definite article, used absolutely as a divine title before YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ (not ʾăḏōnāy H136)
newEntries.partOfSpeech: noun (masculine singular, definite), divine title in apposition
newEntries.standardEnglish: the Sovereign (NRSV; NJPS, checked against Sefaria at 10:16, 33); the Lord (ASV, KJV, which give ʾāḏôn and ʾăḏōnāy the same English)
newEntries.wohChoice: 'the Sovereign' for hā-ʾāḏôn, the articular title before 'YHWH of hosts', at every Isaiah site: 1:24 'the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel'; 3:1 'the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts'; and the later sites 10:16, 10:33 and 19:4. The title ʾăḏōnāy (adonai-standalone-title-isaiah) and the compound ʾăḏōnāy YHWH (adonai-yhwh-compound-isaiah-25) stay 'the Lord'. Commentary names the Hebrew hā-ʾāḏôn at each site. Founder ruling 2026-11-26 (wave I-1 decision 1, option B).
newEntries.rationale: Isaiah uses two different words that English traditionally renders 'the Lord': the title ʾăḏōnāy, a plural of majesty with a fossilised suffix (6:1, 8, 11; 29:13; 3:17, 18; overlay adonai-standalone-title-isaiah), and the common noun ʾāḏôn 'lord, master' with the article, hā-ʾāḏôn, which occurs in the book only in a fixed formula before YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ (1:24; 3:1; 10:16, 33; 19:4; cf. Exod 23:17; 34:23 hā-ʾāḏōn YHWH). Neither the ʾăḏōnāy entry nor the compound entry adonai-yhwh-compound-isaiah-25 covers the articular form. hā-ʾāḏôn is a royal or proprietary title, the master who owns and commands (HALOT s.v. ʾāḏôn; Jenni, TLOT 1:23-29; Eissfeldt, TDOT 1:59-72). Three standard renderings were weighed: ASV and KJV 'the Lord', which is accurate but gives ʾāḏôn and ʾăḏōnāy the same English; 'the Master', the literal sense, which is less idiomatic as a divine title; and 'the Sovereign', used by NRSV and NJPS (NJPS checked at 10:16, 33). The founder ruling of 2026-11-26 adopts 'the Sovereign', because the book's divine-name house style keeps distinct Hebrew titles distinct in English, and this rendering makes the difference visible in the line, not only in the commentary. The claim is direct: every option is a standard rendering of the noun and no lens is involved. This entry absorbs ha-adon-definite-title-isaiah, proposed for 3:1 by the chapter 3 Editor (merged at the wave I-1 merge, appliesTo united). The sites 10:16 and 10:33 are added by the wave I-3 diffs; 19:4 takes the same rendering when that chapter is translated.

newEntries.strongs: H424 (ʾēlāh); H352 (ʾayil III, pl. ʾêlîm 'great trees, terebinths'); H437 (ʾallôn)
newEntries.lemma: tree names: ʾēlāh / ʾayil 'terebinth' (Pistacia) and ʾallôn 'oak' (Quercus)
newEntries.wohChoice: 'terebinth' for ʾēlāh and 'terebinths' for ʾêlîm (1:29, 30; 6:13 'like the terebinth'); 'oak' for ʾallôn (6:13 'and like the oak'; 44:14; 2:13 'the oaks of Bashan').
newEntries.rationale: Hebrew distinguishes ʾēlāh (with the related ʾayil, plural ʾêlîm), the terebinth Pistacia atlantica / palaestina, from ʾallôn, the oak (HALOT; Zohary, Plants of the Bible, 1982; Hepper, Illustrated Encyclopedia of Bible Plants, 1992). The ASV and NRSV render both 'oak' at 1:29-30, which erases the distinction that 6:13 depends on ('like the terebinth and like the oak'), where the signed-off overlay already prints the two names separately (levaer-massevet-stump-isaiah). NJPS renders 'terebinths / terebinth' at 1:29-30. Using one English word per Hebrew tree name keeps the book consistent and lets readers see that the trees of the cultic sites in 1:29 are the same species as the felled tree of 6:13. The claim is direct because the botanical identification is lexical consensus and the change adds no interpretation.

newEntries.lemma: single-site lexical and syntactic decisions of Isaiah 1
newEntries.literal: they rebelled against me; on what?; daughter of Zion; watched; a survivor, a little; incense / smoke; your appointed times; set right the oppressed/ruthless; let us dispute; I will relieve myself; as (with) cleanness / lye; your tin; her returning ones; the strong; tow; its maker (participle, as pointed) / his work (noun, repointed)
newEntries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout, with NRSV/NJPS alternatives as listed in wohChoice
newEntries.wohChoice: 1:2 pāšʿû bî 'they have rebelled against me' (ASV, NRSV, NJPS; 43:27 'transgressed' is kept there); 1:28 pōšʿîm 'transgressors' (ASV), keeping pšʿ distinct from sôrᵉrîm 'rebels' (1:23); 1:5 ʿal meh 'Why' (ASV; locative 'on what part?' in commentary); 1:8 baṯ-ṣiyyôn 'the daughter of Zion' (corpus wording; appositional sense in commentary) and nᵉṣûrāh 'besieged' (nṣr in the blockade sense, Jer 4:16); 1:9 śārîḏ kimʿāṭ 'a very small remnant' following the accents (central she-erit NOT applied: śārîḏ is not šᵉʾērîṯ); 1:13 qᵉṭōreṯ 'incense' (ASV); 1:14 môʿăḏêḵem 'your appointed feasts' (ASV; central moadim NOT extended); 1:17 ʾaššᵉrû ḥāmôṣ 'relieve the oppressed' (LXX, Vulgate, ASV, NRSV, NJPS; active 'correct the oppressor' in commentary); 1:18 wᵉniwwāḵᵉḥāh 'let us reason together' (ASV; forensic sense in commentary) with the conditionals as promises; 1:24 ʾennāḥēm miṣṣāray 'I will ease myself of my adversaries' (ASV); 1:25 kabbōr 'thoroughly' (ASV; 'as with lye' in commentary) and bᵉḏîlāyiḵ 'your tin' (ASV; 'alloy' in commentary); 1:27 wᵉšāḇêhā 'those of her who return' (ambiguity of šûḇ kept); 1:31 he-ḥāsōn 'the strong', nᵉʿōreṯ 'tinder' (NRSV, NJPS; ASV 'tow'), ûp̄ōʿălô 'its maker', following the MT pointing of the suffixed Qal participle pōʿēl (Job 36:3 lᵉp̄ōʿălî 'to my Maker'); 'his work' (ASV, NRSV, on the repointing pāʿŏlô) in commentary (founder ruling 2026-11-26).
newEntries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator's draft follows the ASV and the modern versions or lexica offer a defensible alternative. The Editor keeps the standard rendering in the line where it is supported by the Masoretic consonants and accents, by the ancient versions, or by the lexica, and reports the alternative in commentary, so that the text stays a conventional scholarly rendering and the apparatus shows the choice. (1) pšʿ: the verb with bᵉ- of a person is breach of a relationship (Knierim, TLOT 2:1033-1037); 'rebelled' suits the parent-child frame of 1:2, while 'transgressors' at 1:28 avoids collapsing pšʿ, srr (1:23) and mrh (1:20) into one English word. (2) 1:9 follows the athnach, as ASV does; śārîḏ is a survivor (BDB, HALOT), not the remnant-keyword governed by the central she-erit entry. (3) 1:17: both ancient versions read ḥāmôṣ as passive (LXX rhysasthe adikoumenon; Vulgate subvenite oppresso), while BDB's 'ruthless' supports the active reading of RSV; the versions decide. (4) 1:18: ykḥ Niphal is forensic (HALOT 'argue a case'); 'reason together' is kept as the established English and the court setting is stated in the note. (5) 1:25: bōr is either 'cleanness' (ASV 'thoroughly') or 'lye' (HALOT, NRSV, NJPS); both are lexically attested, and the ASV is kept under the rule that a correct draft is preserved. (6) 1:31: the Masoretic vowels of ûp̄ōʿălô (holem, hatef patah) are those of the suffixed Qal participle, as at Job 36:3, whereas the noun pōʿal with suffix is pointed pāʿŏlô (Jer 22:13; Prov 20:11). Under the book's rule that the line translates the pointed MT (applied at 1:12), the line reads 'and its maker a spark', and the noun reading 'his work' of ASV and NRSV, which presupposes a repointing, is reported in commentary (founder ruling 2026-11-26, wave I-1 decision 3). No item carries a project-specific reading, so the claim type is direct.
